newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian communist leader freed from house arrest.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian communist leader freed from house arrest.

text.p: Bulgaria's former communist leader, Todor Zhivkov, was freed from house arrest on Monday, Sofia prosecutor Mikhail Donchev said.
The release of Zhivkov, 85, occurred amid a deepening economic and political crisis and two days before President Zhelyu Zhelev, an anti-communist, is due to hand over to successor Petar Stoyanov.
Doichev told Reuters he had written the order following a decision from the chief prosecutor's office.
"He is an old man, and in view of his health he should be free to move round town," Doichev said.
Doichev said Zhivkov was obliged to inform the prosecutor's office if he wanted to leave Sofia or change his residence.
Zhivkov was convicted in 1992 of embezzling 21.5 million levs (then about $24 million) of public funds, spent on luxury apartments and Western cars for his family and favoured aides.
Last February the Supreme Court overturned the sentence but he still needed permission to leave his granddaughter's villa in Sofia's wealthy Boyana suburb.
"From today Todor Zhivkov can go wherever he wants," national television said.
"I haven't heard a report in the press," Zhivkov told the television. "If he has signed something, it is still on its way and it will probably take two years to reach me."
Zhivkov ruled Bulgaria for 35 years until the collapse of his hardline communist administration in 1989.
He is one of Eastern Europe's last surviving communist leaders.
Zhelev, a dissident philosopher, was appointed president in August 1990 and won an election in 1992.

Despite allegations of corruption, Zhivkov remains popular among many Bulgarians nostalgic for the simpler days of one- party rule when the state ensured cheap bread while hindering freedom of speech and movement.
